reason: The sources provide detailed, multi-sourced facts tracking the rise and resolution of 2024 YR4's Earth and lunar impact threats.
story: In late December 2024, astronomers discovered asteroid 2024 YR4 just two days after it passed Earth. Initial orbit calculations revealed an alarming prospect: a greater than 3% chance of striking Earth on December 22, 2032. Reaching a rating of 3 on the Torino scale, it became the second-highest rated impact threat in history, behind only Apophis. Measuring between 53 and 67 meters wide—comparable to the object behind the 1908 Tunguska explosion—its estimated risk corridor stretched across South America, the Atlantic, and sub-Saharan Africa. By March 2025, follow-up observations ruled out an Earth collision, but left a lingering 4% chance the asteroid would smash into the Moon instead. Finally, in early 2026, infrared tracking from the James Webb Space Telescope officially eliminated the lunar impact threat as well, confirming 2024 YR4 will safely pass both Earth and the Moon.
angle: After astronomers ruled out 2024 YR4 hitting Earth in 2032, the space rock still held a 4% chance of crashing into the Moon on the exact same day.

claims.claim: Asteroid 2024 YR4 was discovered by the ATLAS station in Río Hurtado, Chile on December 27, 2024.
The asteroid was discovered two days after it had already made a close pass by Earth.
Automated tracking systems initially identified a risk of 2024 YR4 colliding with Earth on December 22, 2032.
In February 2025, the estimated probability of 2024 YR4 impacting Earth peaked above 3 percent.
2024 YR4 reached a rating of 3 on the Torino impact hazard scale.
A Torino scale rating of 3 is the second-highest rating ever assigned to an asteroid, behind only 99942 Apophis.
Infrared thermal measurements by the James Webb Space Telescope established the asteroid's diameter at 53 to 67 meters (174 to 220 feet).
2024 YR4 is approximately the same size as the space rock responsible for the 1908 Tunguska event.
Due to its size and stony composition, an atmospheric entry by 2024 YR4 would most likely produce a high-altitude airburst.
The calculated Earth impact risk corridor stretched across South America, the Atlantic Ocean, and sub-Saharan Africa.
By March 2025, additional tracking observations allowed scientists to completely rule out an Earth impact in 2032.
After an Earth impact was ruled out, data showed a lingering 4 percent chance the asteroid would strike the Moon on December 22, 2032.
Follow-up observations by the James Webb Space Telescope in early 2026 reduced the lunar impact probability to zero percent.
A lunar collision by 2024 YR4 would have excavated a crater up to 1.2 to 2 kilometers wide on the Moon.
2024 YR4 will make its next close approach to Earth in December 2028.

disputed: Calculated lunar impact odds prior to 2026 JWST observations varied between sources (S1 and S3 report around 4%, while S6 reports 0.3%); a script should frame this as an evolving statistical calculation.

Visibility of a potential lunar impact from Earth was debated (S1 notes SETI scientist Michael Busch doubted naked-eye visibility due to lunar glare, while S1, S3, and S6 cite astronomers stating the flash could be brighter than the full moon); a script should attribute these opinions directly.
